# ferridriver_test_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-test-macros/0.5.0/ferridriver_test_macros/

## Expand description

Proc macros for the ferridriver test framework.

Provides `#[ferritest]` to register async browser test functions. The
annotated function takes a single `TestContext`; built-in fixtures
(`page`, `browser`, `context`, …) resolve lazily through it.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver_test::prelude::*;
#[ferritest]
async fn basic_navigation(ctx: TestContext) {
    let page = ctx.page().await?;
    page.goto("https://example.com", None).await?;
    expect(&page).to_have_title("Example").await?;
}
#[ferritest(retries = 2, timeout = "30s", tag = "smoke")]
async fn flaky_test(ctx: TestContext) {
    let page = ctx.page().await?;
    let context = ctx.browser_context().await?;
    // ...
}
```
## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [after_](https://docs.rs/attr.after_all.html)- all
- Runs once after all tests in the containing module (suite).
- [after_](https://docs.rs/attr.after_each.html)- each
- Runs after each test in the containing module (suite), even on failure.
- [before_](https://docs.rs/attr.before_all.html)- all
- Runs once before all tests in the containing module (suite).
- [before_](https://docs.rs/attr.before_each.html)- each
- Runs before each test in the containing module (suite).
- [ferritest](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest.html)
- `#[ferritest]`attribute macro.
- [ferritest_](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest_each.html)- each
- `#[ferritest_each(data = [("a", 1), ("b", 2)])]`— parameterized test macro.
- [ferritest_](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest_suite.html)- suite
- `#[ferritest_suite(mode = "serial")]`— set the execution mode of every- `#[ferritest]`in the annotated module. A serial suite is dispatched as one batch to a single worker, runs in source order, and skips the rest on first failure. The default (no attribute) is parallel.
- [fixture](https://docs.rs/attr.fixture.html)
- `#[fixture]`— register a custom, dependency-injected, scoped fixture.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buckets](https://docs.rs/buckets/index.html)
- Bucketing + pure estimation — the model-blind feature layer.
- [builtin_](https://docs.rs/builtin_rates/index.html)- rates
- Built-in per-model token rates (shipped baseline).
- [calibration](https://docs.rs/calibration/index.html)
- Calibration — the pure ridge-regression math that turns observed
(text, realTokens) rounds into per-bucket rates. Model-blind and stateless;
the stateful writer/reader wrappers live in `calibrator`/`estimator`.
- [calibrator](https://docs.rs/calibrator/index.html)
- TokenCalibrator (writer) — the stateful producer side. Wraps ONE model’s
data-only accumulator: feed it real usage via `observe`, read back solved`rates()`or the raw`to_matrix()`for persistence.
- [estimator](https://docs.rs/estimator/index.html)
- TokenEstimator (reader) — the stateful consumer side (renderer / CLI display).
Built from a `{model: matrix}`map; derives + caches each model’s rates up front. Pure math is in`calibration`; this is per-model lookup plus the shipped-baseline fallback.

# awsm_renderer_gltf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-gltf/0.12.0/awsm_renderer_gltf/

## Expand description

glTF ingestion for `awsm-renderer`.

Extracted from `awsm-renderer` as part of the editor-renderer overhaul.
glTF is one ingestion path into the renderer’s public raw-mesh API; it
is not privileged. Any other format (USD, custom, procedural) consumes
the same renderer surface this crate uses.

Loading flow:

- `loader::load_gltf`(async) fetches- `.gltf`/- `.glb`+ external buffers / images, parses into a- `GltfData`.
- `AwsmRenderer::populate_gltf(...)`(via the- `AwsmRendererGltfExt`extension trait below) walks the parsed scene and uploads meshes, materials, textures, animations, skins, transforms into the renderer.
- The caller gets back a `GltfKeyLookups`mapping per-document glTF indices to renderer keys (mesh / material / transform / animation).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# awsm_renderer_gltf_convert - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-gltf-convert/0.12.0/awsm_renderer_gltf_convert/

## Expand description

Pure-data glTF → canonical AWSM-format conversion.

This is the single import/convert path (see `docs/buffers.md`). It runs entirely on bytes — no GPU,
no browser, no renderer — so it’s exhaustively property-testable. Both the
editor and the player call [ convert](https://docs.rs/fn.convert.html) before any population:

```
foreign glTF ──convert──▶ self-contained canonical glb (geometry + materials
                          + textures, AWSM_format-stamped)
                          + extracted material / animation specs (for the bridge)
our own glb (AWSM_format) ──convert──▶ passed through unchanged
```
The [ AWSM_FORMAT](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_FORMAT.html) extension marker makes the round-trip idempotent:
converting our own export is a no-op (

`convert(convert(x)) == convert(x)`).[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-status-overnight-phase-3--see-the-plan-doc)Implementation status (overnight Phase 3 — see the plan doc)

Increment 1 (this file): crate + `AWSM_FORMAT` + detection + the geometry
conversion (clean glb via `glb-export`’s `reexport_clean_scene`/`write_glb`).
FOLLOW-ON increments, each its own commit:

- stamp `AWSM_FORMAT`onto the output glb (needs a`glb-export`writer hook) → unlocks the idempotency pass-through + its proptest;
- bake tangents + ensure normals into the canonical glb (needs
`MeshData.tangents`+ a`TANGENT`accessor in`glb-export::write_glb`);
- extract materials + animations (move the pure logic out of the editor
bridge: `extract_material_specs`/`extract_extensions`/`extract_animations`).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use animations::`- [extract_animations](https://docs.rs/animations/fn.extract_animations.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [AnimChannel](https://docs.rs/animations/struct.AnimChannel.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [AnimProperty](https://docs.rs/animations/enum.AnimProperty.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [AnimationSpec](https://docs.rs/animations/struct.AnimationSpec.html);
- `pub use animations::`- [Interpolation](https://docs.rs/animations/enum.Interpolation.html);
- `pub use images::`- [extract_images](https://docs.rs/images/fn.extract_images.html);
- `pub use images::`- [ImageData](https://docs.rs/images/struct.ImageData.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [extract_extensions](https://docs.rs/materials/fn.extract_extensions.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [extract_materials](https://docs.rs/materials/fn.extract_materials.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [AlphaMode](https://docs.rs/materials/enum.AlphaMode.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [Clearcoat](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.Clearcoat.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [ExtTextureSlot](https://docs.rs/materials/enum.ExtTextureSlot.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [Iridescence](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.Iridescence.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [MaterialExtensions](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.MaterialExtensions.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [MaterialSpec](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.MaterialSpec.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [Sheen](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.Sheen.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [TexRef](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.TexRef.html);
- `pub use materials::`- [Volume](https://docs.rs/materials/struct.Volume.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [animations](https://docs.rs/animations/index.html)
- Animation extraction — reads a source glTF’s animations into NEUTRAL specs
(raw sampler data: times + flattened output values + interpolation), keyed by
glTF node index. Pure glTF reading via the crate’s animation channel reader —
no renderer types (renderer-gltf’s `extract_animations`produces renderer`AnimationClip`s and so can’t live here). The editor/player map node_index → NodeId and lower the sampler into their own keyframes at the wiring step.
- [images](https://docs.rs/images/index.html)
- Texture-image extraction — pulls the RAW encoded image bytes (PNG/JPEG) out
of a glTF, indexed by glTF image index (the index `materials::TexRef.image`points at). Raw (not decoded) so the editor can write them straight to`assets/<id>.png`and the player decodes on GPU upload, same as it would from a bundle file. Pure data — no decode, no I/O.
- [materials](https://docs.rs/materials/index.html)
- Material extraction — reads a source glTF’s materials into NEUTRAL specs,
decoupled from both editor-protocol and scene types (each maps at its own
wiring step). Pure glTF reading; no GPU, no image upload (texture *image*bytes are pure data shipped separately; refs here point at glTF image indices).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Canonical](https://docs.rs/struct.CanonicalImport.html)- Import
- The result of `convert`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Convert](https://docs.rs/enum.ConvertError.html)- Error
- Conversion failures (all pure-data; no I/O).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [AWSM_](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_FORMAT.html)- FORMAT
- Document-level glTF extension stamped onto a canonical AWSM glb. Its presence means “this glb was produced by our exporter / converter and is already in canonical form” — re-converting it is a no-op. Carries a version so a future canonical-form change is detectable rather than silently mis-read.
- [AWSM_](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_FORMAT_VERSION.html)- FORMAT_ - VERSION
- Current canonical-form version stamped under `AWSM_FORMAT``version`field.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [awsm_](https://docs.rs/fn.awsm_format_version.html)- format_ - version
- Read the `AWSM_format`version from an already-canonical document, if present.
- [convert](https://docs.rs/fn.convert.html)
- Normalize arbitrary glTF/GLB bytes to the canonical AWSM form.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_canonical.html)- canonical
- Does this parsed document carry the `AWSM_FORMAT`
- [stamp_](https://docs.rs/fn.stamp_awsm_format.html)- awsm_ - format
- Inject the `AWSM_FORMAT``extensionsUsed`and a document-level`extensions.AWSM_format = { version }`. Pure byte/JSON surgery on the JSON chunk (the BIN chunk is untouched), so the result re-parses as a normal glTF that`is_canonical`

# awsm_renderer_lod_bake - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-lod-bake/0.12.0/awsm_renderer_lod_bake/

## Expand description

`awsm-renderer-lod-bake` — offline LOD bake over plain geometry arrays.

Pure Rust, no GPU, **wasm-safe** (the bake runs inside the editor frontend,
a `wasm32-unknown-unknown` crate, so a C simplifier like meshoptimizer is not
an option — Apple clang has no wasm target). The shared primitive is a
boundary-locked half-edge QEM collapse ([`simplify`]) that keeps the
surviving vertices a *subset* of the originals, so per-vertex attributes
(skin weights, morph deltas, …) carry through a level verbatim.

Phase A (discrete LOD chain) uses [ build_lod_chain](https://docs.rs/simplify/fn.build_lod_chain.html); Phase B (cluster LOD
DAG) will reuse the same collapse with locked group boundaries.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use cluster::`- [build_cluster_graph](https://docs.rs/cluster/fn.build_cluster_graph.html);
- `pub use cluster::`- [build_clusters](https://docs.rs/cluster/fn.build_clusters.html);
- `pub use cluster::`- [group_clusters](https://docs.rs/cluster/fn.group_clusters.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cluster](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)
- Cluster (meshlet) generation for the cluster-LOD DAG (Phase B).
- [cluster_](https://docs.rs/cluster_mesh/index.html)- mesh
- Serializable cluster-LOD bake output (Phase B, B.1d): a shared vertex buffer
plus per-cluster **index pages**and meta, ready to upload as GPU buffers and evaluate the LOD cut on-device (B.2/B.3).
- [dag](https://docs.rs/dag/index.html)
- Cluster LOD DAG build (Phase B, B.1c).
- [manifest](https://docs.rs/manifest/index.html)
- The per-mesh LOD descriptor written into the player bundle alongside the level geometry, and read back by the runtime to drive level selection.
- [plan](https://docs.rs/plan/index.html)
- Discrete LOD-chain planning: decide *which*levels to emit for a mesh and describe them, without touching any file format. The caller (the editor bake) turns each`PlannedLevel``LodPlan::manifest`
- [quadric](https://docs.rs/quadric/index.html)
- Symmetric 4×4 error quadric (Garland–Heckbert QEM), stored as its 10 unique
upper-triangular entries. All math is `f64`for numerical stability across many accumulated planes; callers cast the final error to`f32`.
- [simplify](https://docs.rs/simplify/index.html)
- Boundary-locked half-edge QEM simplification.

# awsm_renderer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer/0.12.0/awsm_renderer/

## Expand description

High-level renderer API and shared modules.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-scene-schema-feature-optional-schema--runtime-bridge)The `scene-schema` feature (optional schema → runtime bridge)

[ awsm-renderer-scene](https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-scene) is the pure-data,
on-disk authoring format (

`EditorProject`, saved as `project.json`). The
renderer holds the *runtime*equivalents of those types. Enabling the

`scene-schema` feature pulls in `awsm-renderer-scene` (an optional dep) and
compiles a set of `From<awsm_renderer_scene::*>` impls so a consumer can convert
authored data into renderer config with a single `.into()`:[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let project: awsm_renderer_scene::EditorProject = serde_json::from_str(&text)?;
renderer.set_shadows_config(project.shadows.into());
```
It is **off by default**: a bare runtime consumer never pays for the schema
crate, and the editor frontends keep their own bridges. It exists mainly for
standalone *players* that load `EditorProject` bundles and want first-party
conversion that lives next to the runtime structs (so it can never drift).

[§](https://docs.rs#adding-more-conversions)Adding more conversions

This is an **extension point**, not a one-off. Today the only bridge is
shadows (`shadows::schema_convert`, gated by `#[cfg(feature = "scene-schema")]`). To bridge another subsystem (environment, lights,
materials, …), add a feature-gated `schema_convert` module beside that
subsystem’s runtime types and write the `From` impls there, following
`shadows::schema_convert` as the template. Keeping each bridge next to the
structs it maps is what stops the conversions from rotting.

- `pub use load_phase::`- [LoadPhase](https://docs.rs/load_phase/enum.LoadPhase.html);
- `pub use loading::`- [LoadPhase](https://docs.rs/loading/enum.LoadPhase.html)as CommitLoadPhase;

When the resolved value is non-zero, the next render preamble calls`crate::AwsmRenderer::set_max_per_froxel_capacity``(current * 2)`so subsequent frames have headroom. Single-buffered (`inflight`gates the next kick).

# proc-macro2 1.0.106 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/1.0.106

# proc-macro2

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler's `proc_macro` crate.
This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

## Usage

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you'll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to propagate
parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

## Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable compiler
API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not exposed by
proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly compiler,
the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to rustc. We will
polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As these are unstable APIs
that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of proc-macro2 may make breaking
changes to them at any time.

```
RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build
```

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

---

                    proc-macro2 1.0.106

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/1.0.106/target-redirect/proc_macro2/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# proc-macro2

                    There is very little structured metadata to build this page
                    from currently. You should check the

[main library docs](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/),[readme](https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/1.0.106), or[Cargo.toml](https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/1.0.106/source/Cargo.toml.orig)in case the author documented the features in them.This version has **3** feature flags, **1** of them enabled by **default**.

### default

### proc-macro (default)

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

### nightly

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

### span-locations

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# lib.rs - source

# proc_macro2/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! [![github]](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro2) [![crates-io]](https://crates.io/crates/proc-macro2) [![docs-rs]](crate)
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [github]: https://img.shields.io/badge/github-8da0cb?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=github
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [crates-io]: https://img.shields.io/badge/crates.io-fc8d62?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=rust
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! [docs-rs]: https://img.shields.io/badge/docs.rs-66c2a5?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=docs.rs
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! <br>
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler's [`proc_macro`]
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! crate. This library serves two purposes:
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! - **Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!   main.rs.** Types from `proc_macro` are entirely specific to procedural
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!   macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!   Meanwhile `proc_macro2` types may exist anywhere including non-macro code.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!   By developing foundational libraries like [syn] and [quote] against
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!   `proc_macro2` rather than `proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!   reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - **Make procedural macros unit testable.** As a consequence of being
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!   specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses `proc_macro` can be
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!   a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!   `proc_macro2`.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! [syn]: https://github.com/dtolnay/syn
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [quote]: https://github.com/dtolnay/quote
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! # Usage
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! extern crate proc_macro;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! # const IGNORE: &str = stringify! {
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! #[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! # };
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! # #[cfg(wrap_proc_macro)]
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!         /* transform input */
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!         # input
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     };
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! }
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! If parsing with [Syn], you'll use [`parse_macro_input!`] instead to
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! [`parse_macro_input!`]: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! # Unstable features
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! exposed by proc-macro2 by default.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! ```sh
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! ```
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! # Thread-Safety
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! a different thread.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)
[86](https://docs.rs#86)#![no_std]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106")]

[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

[255](https://docs.rs#255)
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// Attempts to break the string into tokens and parse those tokens into a token
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// stream.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// May fail for a number of reasons, for example, if the string contains
[260](https://docs.rs#260)/// unbalanced delimiters or characters not existing in the language.
[261](https://docs.rs#261)///
[262](https://docs.rs#262)/// NOTE: Some errors may cause panics instead of returning `LexError`. We
[263](https://docs.rs#263)/// reserve the right to change these errors into `LexError`s later.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)impl [FromStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html) for [TokenStream](https://docs.rs#211-214) {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    type Err = [LexError](https://docs.rs#217-220);
[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    fn from_str(src: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[TokenStream](https://docs.rs#211-214), [LexError](https://docs.rs#217-220)> {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        match imp::[TokenStream](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#25-28)::[from_str_checked](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#98-108)([src](https://docs.rs#267)) {

[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// Convert `proc_macro2::Span` to `proc_macro::Span`.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// This method is available when building with a nightly compiler, or when
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    /// building with rustc 1.29+ *without* semver exempt features.
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    ///
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// # Panics
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    ///
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// Panics if called from outside of a procedural macro. Unlike
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    /// `proc_macro2::Span`, the `proc_macro::Span` type can only exist within
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// the context of a procedural macro invocation.
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    #[cfg(wrap_proc_macro)]
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    pub fn unwrap(self) -> proc_macro::[Span](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/struct.Span.html) {
[459](https://docs.rs#459)        [self](https://docs.rs#458).inner.[unwrap](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#423-428)()
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    }
[461](https://docs.rs#461)
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    // Soft deprecated. Please use Span::unwrap.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    #[cfg(wrap_proc_macro)]
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    #[doc(hidden)]
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    pub fn unstable(self) -> proc_macro::[Span](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/struct.Span.html) {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        [self](https://docs.rs#465).[unwrap](https://docs.rs#458-460)()
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    }
[468](https://docs.rs#468)
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// Returns the span's byte position range in the source file.
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    ///
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    /// This method requires the `"span-locations"` feature to be enabled.
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    ///
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    /// When executing in a procedural macro context, the returned range is only
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    /// accurate if compiled with a nightly toolchain. The stable toolchain does
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    /// not have this information available. When executing outside of a
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// procedural macro, such as main.rs or build.rs, the byte range is always
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    /// accurate regardless of toolchain.
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    #[cfg(span_locations)]

[576](https://docs.rs#576)/// A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

[655](https://docs.rs#655)/// Prints token tree in a form convenient for debugging.
[656](https://docs.rs#656)impl [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) for [TokenTree](https://docs.rs#578-587) {
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::[Formatter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/struct.Formatter.html)) -> fmt::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/type.Result.html) {
[658](https://docs.rs#658)        // Each of these has the name in the struct type in the derived debug,

[662](https://docs.rs#662)            TokenTree::[Ident](https://docs.rs#582)(t) => {
[663](https://docs.rs#663)                let mut debug = [f](https://docs.rs#657).[debug_struct](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/struct.Formatter.html#method.debug_struct)("Ident");
[664](https://docs.rs#664)                [debug](https://docs.rs#663).[field](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/builders/struct.DebugStruct.html#method.field)("sym", &[format_args!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/macro.format_args.html)("{}", t));

[666](https://docs.rs#666)                [debug](https://docs.rs#663).[finish](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/builders/struct.DebugStruct.html#method.finish)()
[667](https://docs.rs#667)            }

[669](https://docs.rs#669)            TokenTree::[Literal](https://docs.rs#586)(t) => Debug::[fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html#tymethod.fmt)([t](https://docs.rs#669), [f](https://docs.rs#657)),
[670](https://docs.rs#670)        }
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    }
[672](https://docs.rs#672)}
[673](https://docs.rs#673)
[674](https://docs.rs#674)/// A delimited token stream.
[675](https://docs.rs#675)///
[676](https://docs.rs#676)/// A `Group` internally contains a `TokenStream` which is surrounded by
[677](https://docs.rs#677)/// `Delimiter`s.
[678](https://docs.rs#678)#[derive([Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html))]
[679](https://docs.rs#679)pub struct [Group](https://docs.rs/proc_macro2/struct.Group.html) {
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    inner: imp::[Group](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#562-565),
[681](https://docs.rs#681)}
[682](https://docs.rs#682)
[683](https://docs.rs#683)/// Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
[684](https://docs.rs#684)#[derive([Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/derive.Copy.html), [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html), [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/macros/derive.Debug.html), [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cmp/derive.Eq.html), [PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cmp/derive.PartialEq.html))]
[685](https://docs.rs#685)pub enum [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/proc_macro2/enum.Delimiter.html) {
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// `( ... )`
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    Parenthesis,
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// `{ ... }`
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    Brace,
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// `[ ... ]`
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    Bracket,
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    /// `∅ ... ∅`
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    ///
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    /// An invisible delimiter, that may, for example, appear around tokens
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// coming from a "macro variable" `$var`. It is important to preserve
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    /// operator priorities in cases like `$var * 3` where `$var` is `1 + 2`.
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// Invisible delimiters may not survive roundtrip of a token stream through
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// a string.
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    ///
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    /// <div class="warning">
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    ///
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// Note: rustc currently can ignore the grouping of tokens delimited by `None` in the output
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    /// of a proc_macro. Only `None`-delimited groups created by a macro_rules macro in the input
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    /// of a proc_macro macro are preserved, and only in very specific circumstances.
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    /// Any `None`-delimited groups (re)created by a proc_macro will therefore not preserve
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// operator priorities as indicated above. The other `Delimiter` variants should be used
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    /// instead in this context. This is a rustc bug. For details, see
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    /// [rust-lang/rust#67062](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/67062).
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    ///
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    /// </div>
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    None,
[712](https://docs.rs#712)}
[713](https://docs.rs#713)
[714](https://docs.rs#714)impl [Group](https://docs.rs#679-681) {
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    fn _new(inner: imp::[Group](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#562-565)) -> Self {
[716](https://docs.rs#716)        [Group](https://docs.rs#679-681) { [inner](https://docs.rs#715) }
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    }
[718](https://docs.rs#718)
[719](https://docs.rs#719)    fn _new_fallback(inner: fallback::[Group](https://docs.rs/fallback.rs.html#719-723)) -> Self {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)        [Group](https://docs.rs#679-681) {
[721](https://docs.rs#721)            inner: imp::[Group](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#562-565)::[from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from)([inner](https://docs.rs#719)),
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        }
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    }
[724](https://docs.rs#724)
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    /// Creates a new `Group` with the given delimiter and token stream.
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    ///
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    /// This constructor will set the span for this group to
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    /// `Span::call_site()`. To change the span you can use the `set_span`
[729](https://docs.rs#729)    /// method below.
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    pub fn new(delimiter: [Delimiter](https://docs.rs#685-712), stream: [TokenStream](https://docs.rs#211-214)) -> Self {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)        [Group](https://docs.rs#679-681) {
[732](https://docs.rs#732)            inner: imp::[Group](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#562-565)::[new](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#568-583)([delimiter](https://docs.rs#730), [stream](https://docs.rs#730).inner),
[733](https://docs.rs#733)        }
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    }

[813](https://docs.rs#813)
[814](https://docs.rs#814)/// A `Punct` is a single punctuation character like `+`, `-` or `#`.
[815](https://docs.rs#815)///
[816](https://docs.rs#816)/// Multicharacter operators like `+=` are represented as two instances of
[817](https://docs.rs#817)/// `Punct` with different forms of `Spacing` returned.
[818](https://docs.rs#818)#[derive([Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html))]
[819](https://docs.rs#819)pub struct [Punct](https://docs.rs/proc_macro2/struct.Punct.html) {
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    ch: [char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.char.html),
[821](https://docs.rs#821)    spacing: [Spacing](https://docs.rs#828-836),
[822](https://docs.rs#822)    span: [Span](https://docs.rs#390-393),
[823](https://docs.rs#823)}
[824](https://docs.rs#824)
[825](https://docs.rs#825)/// Whether a `Punct` is followed immediately by another `Punct` or followed by
[826](https://docs.rs#826)/// another token or whitespace.
[827](https://docs.rs#827)#[derive([Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/derive.Copy.html), [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html), [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/macros/derive.Debug.html), [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cmp/derive.Eq.html), [PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cmp/derive.PartialEq.html))]
[828](https://docs.rs#828)pub enum [Spacing](https://docs.rs/proc_macro2/enum.Spacing.html) {
[829](https://docs.rs#829)    /// E.g. `+` is `Alone` in `+ =`, `+ident` or `+()`.
[830](https://docs.rs#830)    Alone,
[831](https://docs.rs#831)    /// E.g. `+` is `Joint` in `+=` or `'` is `Joint` in `'#`.
[832](https://docs.rs#832)    ///
[833](https://docs.rs#833)    /// Additionally, single quote `'` can join with identifiers to form
[834](https://docs.rs#834)    /// lifetimes `'ident`.
[835](https://docs.rs#835)    Joint,
[836](https://docs.rs#836)}
[837](https://docs.rs#837)
[838](https://docs.rs#838)impl [Punct](https://docs.rs#819-823) {
[839](https://docs.rs#839)    /// Creates a new `Punct` from the given character and spacing.
[840](https://docs.rs#840)    ///
[841](https://docs.rs#841)    /// The `ch` argument must be a valid punctuation character permitted by the
[842](https://docs.rs#842)    /// language, otherwise the function will panic.
[843](https://docs.rs#843)    ///
[844](https://docs.rs#844)    /// The returned `Punct` will have the default span of `Span::call_site()`
[845](https://docs.rs#845)    /// which can be further configured with the `set_span` method below.
[846](https://docs.rs#846)    pub fn new(ch: [char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.char.html), spacing: [Spacing](https://docs.rs#828-836)) -> Self {
[847](https://docs.rs#847)        if let '!' | '#' | '$' | '%' | '&' | '\'' | '*' | '+' | ',' | '-' | '.' | '/' | ':' | ';'
[848](https://docs.rs#848)        | '<' | '=' | '>' | '?' | '@' | '^' | '|' | '~' = [ch](https://docs.rs#846)
[849](https://docs.rs#849)        {
[850](https://docs.rs#850)            [Punct](https://docs.rs#819-823) {
[851](https://docs.rs#851)                [ch](https://docs.rs#846),
[852](https://docs.rs#852)                [spacing](https://docs.rs#846),
[853](https://docs.rs#853)                span: [Span](https://docs.rs#390-393)::[call_site](https://docs.rs#415-417)(),
[854](https://docs.rs#854)            }
[855](https://docs.rs#855)        } else {
[856](https://docs.rs#856)            [panic!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/macro.panic.html)("unsupported proc macro punctuation character {:?}", ch);
[857](https://docs.rs#857)        }
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    }
[859](https://docs.rs#859)
[860](https://docs.rs#860)    /// Returns the value of this punctuation character as `char`.
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    pub fn as_char(&self) -> [char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.char.html) {
[862](https://docs.rs#862)        [self](https://docs.rs#861).ch
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    }
[864](https://docs.rs#864)
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    /// Returns the spacing of this punctuation character, indicating whether
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    /// it's immediately followed by another `Punct` in the token stream, so
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    /// they can potentially be combined into a multicharacter operator
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    /// (`Joint`), or it's followed by some other token or whitespace (`Alone`)
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    /// so the operator has certainly ended.
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    pub fn spacing(&self) -> [Spacing](https://docs.rs#828-836) {
[871](https://docs.rs#871)        [self](https://docs.rs#870).spacing
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    }
[873](https://docs.rs#873)
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    /// Returns the span for this punctuation character.
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    pub fn span(&self) -> [Span](https://docs.rs#390-393) {
[876](https://docs.rs#876)        [self](https://docs.rs#875).span
[877](https://docs.rs#877)    }
[878](https://docs.rs#878)
[879](https://docs.rs#879)    /// Configure the span for this punctuation character.
[880](https://docs.rs#880)    pub fn set_span(&mut self, span: [Span](https://docs.rs#390-393)) {
[881](https://docs.rs#881)        [self](https://docs.rs#880).span = [span](https://docs.rs#880);
[882](https://docs.rs#882)    }
[883](https://docs.rs#883)}
[884](https://docs.rs#884)
[885](https://docs.rs#885)/// Prints the punctuation character as a string that should be losslessly
[886](https://docs.rs#886)/// convertible back into the same character.
[887](https://docs.rs#887)impl [Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) for [Punct](https://docs.rs#819-823) {
[888](https://docs.rs#888)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::[Formatter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/struct.Formatter.html)) -> fmt::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/type.Result.html) {

[891](https://docs.rs#891)}
[892](https://docs.rs#892)
[893](https://docs.rs#893)impl [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) for [Punct](https://docs.rs#819-823) {
[894](https://docs.rs#894)    fn fmt(&self, fmt: &mut fmt::[Formatter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/struct.Formatter.html)) -> fmt::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/type.Result.html) {
[895](https://docs.rs#895)        let mut debug = [fmt](https://docs.rs#894).[debug_struct](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/struct.Formatter.html#method.debug_struct)("Punct");
[896](https://docs.rs#896)        [debug](https://docs.rs#895).[field](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/builders/struct.DebugStruct.html#method.field)("char", &[self](https://docs.rs#894).ch);
[897](https://docs.rs#897)        [debug](https://docs.rs#895).[field](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/builders/struct.DebugStruct.html#method.field)("spacing", &[self](https://docs.rs#894).spacing);
[898](https://docs.rs#898)        imp::[debug_span_field_if_nontrivial](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#552-559)(&mut [debug](https://docs.rs#895), [self](https://docs.rs#894).span.inner);
[899](https://docs.rs#899)        [debug](https://docs.rs#895).[finish](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/builders/struct.DebugStruct.html#method.finish)()
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    }
[901](https://docs.rs#901)}
[902](https://docs.rs#902)
[903](https://docs.rs#903)/// A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
[904](https://docs.rs#904)///
[905](https://docs.rs#905)/// An identifier consists of at least one Unicode code point, the first of
[906](https://docs.rs#906)/// which has the XID_Start property and the rest of which have the XID_Continue
[907](https://docs.rs#907)/// property.
[908](https://docs.rs#908)///
[909](https://docs.rs#909)/// - The empty string is not an identifier. Use `Option<Ident>`.
[910](https://docs.rs#910)/// - A lifetime is not an identifier. Use `syn::Lifetime` instead.
[911](https://docs.rs#911)///
[912](https://docs.rs#912)/// An identifier constructed with `Ident::new` is permitted to be a Rust
[913](https://docs.rs#913)/// keyword, though parsing one through its [`Parse`] implementation rejects
[914](https://docs.rs#914)/// Rust keywords. Use `input.call(Ident::parse_any)` when parsing to match the
[915](https://docs.rs#915)/// behaviour of `Ident::new`.
[916](https://docs.rs#916)///
[917](https://docs.rs#917)/// [`Parse`]: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/parse/trait.Parse.html
[918](https://docs.rs#918)///
[919](https://docs.rs#919)/// # Examples
[920](https://docs.rs#920)///
[921](https://docs.rs#921)/// A new ident can be created from a string using the `Ident::new` function.
[922](https://docs.rs#922)/// A span must be provided explicitly which governs the name resolution
[923](https://docs.rs#923)/// behavior of the resulting identifier.
[924](https://docs.rs#924)///
[925](https://docs.rs#925)/// ```
[926](https://docs.rs#926)/// use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
[927](https://docs.rs#927)///
[928](https://docs.rs#928)/// fn main() {
[929](https://docs.rs#929)///     let call_ident = Ident::new("calligraphy", Span::call_site());
[930](https://docs.rs#930)///
[931](https://docs.rs#931)///     println!("{}", call_ident);
[932](https://docs.rs#932)/// }
[933](https://docs.rs#933)/// ```
[934](https://docs.rs#934)///
[935](https://docs.rs#935)/// An ident can be interpolated into a token stream using the `quote!` macro.
[936](https://docs.rs#936)///
[937](https://docs.rs#937)/// ```
[938](https://docs.rs#938)/// use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
[939](https://docs.rs#939)/// use quote::quote;
[940](https://docs.rs#940)///
[941](https://docs.rs#941)/// fn main() {
[942](https://docs.rs#942)///     let ident = Ident::new("demo", Span::call_site());
[943](https://docs.rs#943)///
[944](https://docs.rs#944)///     // Create a variable binding whose name is this ident.
[945](https://docs.rs#945)///     let expanded = quote! { let #ident = 10; };
[946](https://docs.rs#946)///
[947](https://docs.rs#947)///     // Create a variable binding with a slightly different name.
[948](https://docs.rs#948)///     let temp_ident = Ident::new(&format!("new_{}", ident), Span::call_site());
[949](https://docs.rs#949)///     let expanded = quote! { let #temp_ident = 10; };
[950](https://docs.rs#950)/// }
[951](https://docs.rs#951)/// ```
[952](https://docs.rs#952)///
[953](https://docs.rs#953)/// A string representation of the ident is available through the `to_string()`
[954](https://docs.rs#954)/// method.
[955](https://docs.rs#955)///
[956](https://docs.rs#956)/// ```
[957](https://docs.rs#957)/// # use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
[958](https://docs.rs#958)/// #
[959](https://docs.rs#959)/// # let ident = Ident::new("another_identifier", Span::call_site());
[960](https://docs.rs#960)/// #
[961](https://docs.rs#961)/// // Examine the ident as a string.
[962](https://docs.rs#962)/// let ident_string = ident.to_string();
[963](https://docs.rs#963)/// if ident_string.len() > 60 {
[964](https://docs.rs#964)///     println!("Very long identifier: {}", ident_string)
[965](https://docs.rs#965)/// }
[966](https://docs.rs#966)/// ```
[967](https://docs.rs#967)#[derive([Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html))]
[968](https://docs.rs#968)pub struct [Ident](https://docs.rs/proc_macro2/struct.Ident.html) {
[969](https://docs.rs#969)    inner: imp::[Ident](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#667-670),
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    _marker: [ProcMacroAutoTraits](https://docs.rs/marker.rs.html#12),
[971](https://docs.rs#971)}
[972](https://docs.rs#972)
[973](https://docs.rs#973)impl [Ident](https://docs.rs#968-971) {
[974](https://docs.rs#974)    fn _new(inner: imp::[Ident](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#667-670)) -> Self {
[975](https://docs.rs#975)        [Ident](https://docs.rs#968-971) {
[976](https://docs.rs#976)            [inner](https://docs.rs#974),
[977](https://docs.rs#977)            _marker: [MARKER](https://docs.rs/marker.rs.html#14),
[978](https://docs.rs#978)        }
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    }
[980](https://docs.rs#980)
[981](https://docs.rs#981)    fn _new_fallback(inner: fallback::[Ident](https://docs.rs/fallback.rs.html#797-801)) -> Self {
[982](https://docs.rs#982)        [Ident](https://docs.rs#968-971) {
[983](https://docs.rs#983)            inner: imp::[Ident](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#667-670)::[from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from)([inner](https://docs.rs#981)),
[984](https://docs.rs#984)            _marker: [MARKER](https://docs.rs/marker.rs.html#14),
[985](https://docs.rs#985)        }
[986](https://docs.rs#986)    }
[987](https://docs.rs#987)
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    /// Creates a new `Ident` with the given `string` as well as the specified
[989](https://docs.rs#989)    /// `span`.
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    ///
[991](https://docs.rs#991)    /// The `string` argument must be a valid identifier permitted by the
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    /// language, otherwise the function will panic.
[993](https://docs.rs#993)    ///
[994](https://docs.rs#994)    /// Note that `span`, currently in rustc, configures the hygiene information
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    /// for this identifier.
[996](https://docs.rs#996)    ///
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    /// As of this time `Span::call_site()` explicitly opts-in to "call-site"
[998](https://docs.rs#998)    /// hygiene meaning that identifiers created with this span will be resolved
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    /// as if they were written directly at the location of the macro call, and
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    /// other code at the macro call site will be able to refer to them as well.
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    ///
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    /// Later spans like `Span::def_site()` will allow to opt-in to
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    /// "definition-site" hygiene meaning that identifiers created with this
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    /// span will be resolved at the location of the macro definition and other
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    /// code at the macro call site will not be able to refer to them.
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)    ///
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)    /// Due to the current importance of hygiene this constructor, unlike other
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)    /// tokens, requires a `Span` to be specified at construction.
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)    ///
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)    /// # Panics
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)    ///
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)    /// Panics if the input string is neither a keyword nor a legal variable
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)    /// name. If you are not sure whether the string contains an identifier and
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)    /// need to handle an error case, use
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)    /// <a href="https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/fn.parse_str.html"><code
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)    ///   style="padding-right:0;">syn::parse_str</code></a><code
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)    ///   style="padding-left:0;">::<Ident></code>
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)    /// rather than `Ident::new`.
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)    #[track_caller]
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)    pub fn new(string: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html), span: [Span](https://docs.rs#390-393)) -> Self {
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)        [Ident](https://docs.rs#968-971)::[_new](https://docs.rs#974-979)(imp::[Ident](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#667-670)::[new_checked](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#674-679)([string](https://docs.rs#1020), [span](https://docs.rs#1020).inner))
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)    }
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)    /// Same as `Ident::new`, but creates a raw identifier (`r#ident`). The
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)    /// `string` argument must be a valid identifier permitted by the language
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)    /// (including keywords, e.g. `fn`). Keywords which are usable in path
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)    /// segments (e.g. `self`, `super`) are not supported, and will cause a
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)    /// panic.
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)    #[track_caller]
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    pub fn new_raw(string: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html), span: [Span](https://docs.rs#390-393)) -> Self {

[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)    }

[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)/// A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`),
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)/// byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)/// a suffix (`1`, `1u8`, `2.3`, `2.3f32`).
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)///
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)/// Boolean literals like `true` and `false` do not belong here, they are
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)/// `Ident`s.
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)#[derive([Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/clone/derive.Clone.html))]
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)pub struct [Literal](https://docs.rs/proc_macro2/struct.Literal.html) {
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)    inner: imp::[Literal](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#762-765),
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)    _marker: [ProcMacroAutoTraits](https://docs.rs/marker.rs.html#12),
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)}
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)macro_rules! suffixed_int_literals {
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)    ($($name:ident => $kind:ident,)*) => ($(
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)        /// Creates a new suffixed integer literal with the specified value.
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)        ///
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)        /// This function will create an integer like `1u32` where the integer
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)        /// value specified is the first part of the token and the integral is
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)        /// also suffixed at the end. Literals created from negative numbers may
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)        /// not survive roundtrips through `TokenStream` or strings and may be
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)        /// broken into two tokens (`-` and positive literal).
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)        ///
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)        /// Literals created through this method have the `Span::call_site()`
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)        /// span by default, which can be configured with the `set_span` method
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)        /// below.
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)        pub fn $name(n: $kind) -> Literal {
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)            Literal::_new(imp::Literal::$name(n))
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)        }
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)    )*)
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)}
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)macro_rules! unsuffixed_int_literals {
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)    ($($name:ident => $kind:ident,)*) => ($(
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)        /// Creates a new unsuffixed integer literal with the specified value.
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)        ///
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)        /// This function will create an integer like `1` where the integer
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)        /// value specified is the first part of the token. No suffix is
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)        /// specified on this token, meaning that invocations like
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)        /// `Literal::i8_unsuffixed(1)` are equivalent to
[1134](https://docs.rs#1134)        /// `Literal::u32_unsuffixed(1)`. Literals created from negative numbers
[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)        /// may not survive roundtrips through `TokenStream` or strings and may
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)        /// be broken into two tokens (`-` and positive literal).
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)        ///
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)        /// Literals created through this method have the `Span::call_site()`
[1139](https://docs.rs#1139)        /// span by default, which can be configured with the `set_span` method
[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)        /// below.
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)        pub fn $name(n: $kind) -> Literal {
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)            Literal::_new(imp::Literal::$name(n))
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)        }
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)    )*)
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)}
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)

[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)    /// Creates a new unsuffixed floating-point literal.
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)    ///
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)    /// This constructor is similar to those like `Literal::i8_unsuffixed` where
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)    /// the float's value is emitted directly into the token but no suffix is
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)    /// used, so it may be inferred to be a `f64` later in the compiler.
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)    /// Literals created from negative numbers may not survive round-trips
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)    /// through `TokenStream` or strings and may be broken into two tokens (`-`
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)    /// and positive literal).
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)    ///
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)    /// # Panics
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)    ///
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)    /// This function requires that the specified float is finite, for example
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)    /// if it is infinity or NaN this function will panic.
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)    pub fn f64_unsuffixed(f: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs#1102-1105) {
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)        [assert!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/macro.assert.html)(f.is_finite());
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)        [Literal](https://docs.rs#1102-1105)::[_new](https://docs.rs#1148-1153)(imp::[Literal](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#762-765)::[f64_unsuffixed](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#851-857)([f](https://docs.rs#1205)))
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)    }
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)    /// Creates a new suffixed floating-point literal.
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)    ///
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)    /// This constructor will create a literal like `1.0f64` where the value
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)    /// specified is the preceding part of the token and `f64` is the suffix of
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)    /// the token. This token will always be inferred to be an `f64` in the
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)    /// compiler. Literals created from negative numbers may not survive
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)    /// round-trips through `TokenStream` or strings and may be broken into two
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)    /// tokens (`-` and positive literal).
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)    ///
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)    /// # Panics
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)    ///
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)    /// This function requires that the specified float is finite, for example
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)    /// if it is infinity or NaN this function will panic.
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)    pub fn f64_suffixed(f: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs#1102-1105) {
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)        [assert!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/macro.assert.html)(f.is_finite());
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)        [Literal](https://docs.rs#1102-1105)::[_new](https://docs.rs#1148-1153)(imp::[Literal](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#762-765)::[f64_suffixed](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#810-826)([f](https://docs.rs#1223)))
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)    }
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)

[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)    /// Creates a new suffixed floating-point literal.

[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    /// tokens (`-` and positive literal).

[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    /// # Panics
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)    ///
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    /// This function requires that the specified float is finite, for example
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    /// if it is infinity or NaN this function will panic.

[1416](https://docs.rs#1416)    // Intended for the `quote!` macro to use when constructing a proc-macro2
[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)    // token out of a macro_rules $:literal token, which is already known to be
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)    // a valid literal. This avoids reparsing/validating the literal's string
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)    // representation. This is not public API other than for quote.
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)    #[doc(hidden)]
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)    pub unsafe fn from_str_unchecked(repr: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)) -> Self {
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)        [Literal](https://docs.rs#1102-1105)::[_new](https://docs.rs#1148-1153)(unsafe { imp::[Literal](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#762-765)::[from_str_unchecked](https://docs.rs/wrapper.rs.html#802-808)([repr](https://docs.rs#1421)) })
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)    }
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)}

# proc_macro2::extra - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/extra/index.html

## Expand description

Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Delim](https://docs.rs/struct.DelimSpan.html)- Span
- An object that holds a `Group``span_open()`and`span_close()`together in a more compact representation than holding those 2 spans individually.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [invalidate_](https://docs.rs/fn.invalidate_current_thread_spans.html)- current_ - thread_ - spans - `span-locations`
- Invalidate any `proc_macro2::Span`that exist on the current thread.

# Group in proc_macro2 - Rust

A delimited token stream.

A `Group` internally contains a `TokenStream` which is surrounded by
`Delimiter`s.

# Ident in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/struct.Ident.html

`pub struct Ident { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.

An identifier consists of at least one Unicode code point, the first of which has the XID_Start property and the rest of which have the XID_Continue property.

- The empty string is not an identifier. Use `Option<Ident>`.
- A lifetime is not an identifier. Use `syn::Lifetime`instead.

An identifier constructed with `Ident::new` is permitted to be a Rust
keyword, though parsing one through its [ Parse](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/parse/trait.Parse.html) implementation rejects
Rust keywords. Use

`input.call(Ident::parse_any)` when parsing to match the
behaviour of `Ident::new`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A new ident can be created from a string using the `Ident::new` function.
A span must be provided explicitly which governs the name resolution
behavior of the resulting identifier.

```
use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
fn main() {
    let call_ident = Ident::new("calligraphy", Span::call_site());
    println!("{}", call_ident);
}
```
An ident can be interpolated into a token stream using the `quote!` macro.

```
use proc_macro2::{Ident, Span};
use quote::quote;
fn main() {
    let ident = Ident::new("demo", Span::call_site());
    // Create a variable binding whose name is this ident.
    let expanded = quote! { let #ident = 10; };
    // Create a variable binding with a slightly different name.
    let temp_ident = Ident::new(&format!("new_{}", ident), Span::call_site());
    let expanded = quote! { let #temp_ident = 10; };
}
```
A string representation of the ident is available through the `to_string()`
method.

```
// Examine the ident as a string.
let ident_string = ident.to_string();
if ident_string.len() > 60 {
    println!("Very long identifier: {}", ident_string)
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `Ident` with the given `string` as well as the specified
`span`.

The `string` argument must be a valid identifier permitted by the
language, otherwise the function will panic.

Note that `span`, currently in rustc, configures the hygiene information
for this identifier.

As of this time `Span::call_site()` explicitly opts-in to “call-site”
hygiene meaning that identifiers created with this span will be resolved
as if they were written directly at the location of the macro call, and
other code at the macro call site will be able to refer to them as well.

Later spans like `Span::def_site()` will allow to opt-in to
“definition-site” hygiene meaning that identifiers created with this
span will be resolved at the location of the macro definition and other
code at the macro call site will not be able to refer to them.

Due to the current importance of hygiene this constructor, unlike other
tokens, requires a `Span` to be specified at construction.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the input string is neither a keyword nor a legal variable
name. If you are not sure whether the string contains an identifier and
need to handle an error case, use
`syn::parse_str``::<Ident>`
rather than `Ident::new`.

Same as `Ident::new`, but creates a raw identifier (`r#ident`). The
`string` argument must be a valid identifier permitted by the language
(including keywords, e.g. `fn`). Keywords which are usable in path
segments (e.g. `self`, `super`) are not supported, and will cause a
panic.

# LineColumn in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/struct.LineColumn.html

**crate feature**only.

`span-locations`## Expand description

A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.

This type is semver exempt and not exposed by default.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.line)

`line: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)The 1-indexed line in the source file on which the span starts or ends (inclusive).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.column)

`column: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)The 0-indexed column (in UTF-8 characters) in the source file on which the span starts or ends (inclusive).

# Literal in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/struct.Literal.html

`pub struct Literal { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`),
byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without
a suffix (`1`, `1u8`, `2.3`, `2.3f32`).

Boolean literals like `true` and `false` do not belong here, they are
`Ident`s.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1162-1175)#### pub fn [u8_suffixed](https://docs.rs#method.u8_suffixed)(n: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1162-1175)

#### pub fn [u8_suffixed](https://docs.rs#method.u8_suffixed)(n: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

Creates a new suffixed integer literal with the specified value.

This function will create an integer like `1u32` where the integer
value specified is the first part of the token and the integral is
also suffixed at the end. Literals created from negative numbers may
not survive roundtrips through `TokenStream` or strings and may be
broken into two tokens (`-` and positive literal).

Literals created through this method have the `Span::call_site()`
span by default, which can be configured with the `set_span` method
below.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1177-1190)#### pub fn [u8_unsuffixed](https://docs.rs#method.u8_unsuffixed)(n: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

#### pub fn [u8_unsuffixed](https://docs.rs#method.u8_unsuffixed)(n: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u8.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

Creates a new unsuffixed integer literal with the specified value.

This function will create an integer like `1` where the integer
value specified is the first part of the token. No suffix is
specified on this token, meaning that invocations like
`Literal::i8_unsuffixed(1)` are equivalent to
`Literal::u32_unsuffixed(1)`. Literals created from negative numbers
may not survive roundtrips through `TokenStream` or strings and may
be broken into two tokens (`-` and positive literal).

Literals created through this method have the `Span::call_site()`
span by default, which can be configured with the `set_span` method
below.

span by default, which can be configured with the `set_span` method
below.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1177-1190)#### pub fn [i8_unsuffixed](https://docs.rs#method.i8_unsuffixed)(n: [i8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i8.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1177-1190)

#### pub fn [i8_unsuffixed](https://docs.rs#method.i8_unsuffixed)(n: [i8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i8.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

Creates a new unsuffixed integer literal with the specified value.

This function will create an integer like `1` where the integer
value specified is the first part of the token. No suffix is
specified on this token, meaning that invocations like
`Literal::i8_unsuffixed(1)` are equivalent to
`Literal::u32_unsuffixed(1)`. Literals created from negative numbers
may not survive roundtrips through `TokenStream` or strings and may
be broken into two tokens (`-` and positive literal).

Literals created through this method have the `Span::call_site()`
span by default, which can be configured with the `set_span` method
below.

#### pub fn [f64_unsuffixed](https://docs.rs#method.f64_unsuffixed)(f: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

Creates a new unsuffixed floating-point literal.

This constructor is similar to those like `Literal::i8_unsuffixed` where
the float’s value is emitted directly into the token but no suffix is
used, so it may be inferred to be a `f64` later in the compiler.
Literals created from negative numbers may not survive round-trips
through `TokenStream` or strings and may be broken into two tokens (`-`
and positive literal).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This function requires that the specified float is finite, for example if it is infinity or NaN this function will panic.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1223-1226)#### pub fn [f64_suffixed](https://docs.rs#method.f64_suffixed)(f: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#1223-1226)

Creates a new suffixed floating-point literal.

This constructor will create a literal like `1.0f64` where the value
specified is the preceding part of the token and `f64` is the suffix of
the token. This token will always be inferred to be an `f64` in the
compiler. Literals created from negative numbers may not survive
round-trips through `TokenStream` or strings and may be broken into two
tokens (`-` and positive literal).

This function requires that the specified float is finite, for example if it is infinity or NaN this function will panic.

# Punct in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/struct.Punct.html

`pub struct Punct { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A `Punct` is a single punctuation character like `+`, `-` or `#`.

Multicharacter operators like `+=` are represented as two instances of
`Punct` with different forms of `Spacing` returned.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `Punct` from the given character and spacing.

The `ch` argument must be a valid punctuation character permitted by the
language, otherwise the function will panic.

The returned `Punct` will have the default span of `Span::call_site()`
which can be further configured with the `set_span` method below.

Returns the spacing of this punctuation character, indicating whether
it’s immediately followed by another `Punct` in the token stream, so
they can potentially be combined into a multicharacter operator
(`Joint`), or it’s followed by some other token or whitespace (`Alone`)
so the operator has certainly ended.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# Span in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0.106/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html

`pub struct Span { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

The span of the invocation of the current procedural macro.

Identifiers created with this span will be resolved as if they were written directly at the macro call location (call-site hygiene) and other code at the macro call site will be able to refer to them as well.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#422-424)#### pub fn [mixed_site](https://docs.rs#method.mixed_site)() -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#422-424)

#### pub fn [mixed_site](https://docs.rs#method.mixed_site)() -> Self

The span located at the invocation of the procedural macro, but with
local variables, labels, and `$crate` resolved at the definition site
of the macro. This is the same hygiene behavior as `macro_rules`.

A span that resolves at the macro definition site.

This method is semver exempt and not exposed by default.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#437-439)#### pub fn [resolved_at](https://docs.rs#method.resolved_at)(&self, other: [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)) -> [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

Creates a new span with the same name resolution behavior as `self` but
with the line/column information of `other`.

Convert `proc_macro2::Span` to `proc_macro::Span`.

This method is available when building with a nightly compiler, or when
building with rustc 1.29+ *without* semver exempt features.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from outside of a procedural macro. Unlike
`proc_macro2::Span`, the `proc_macro::Span` type can only exist within
the context of a procedural macro invocation.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#480-482)#### pub fn [byte_range](https://docs.rs#method.byte_range)(&self) -> [Range](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ops/range/struct.Range.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#480-482)
